Physics hand-checked: I = I₀ cos²θ with θ the angle between the transmission axes of polariser and analyser; at θ = 0° the full intensity I₀ passes, at θ = 90° (crossed) the transmitted intensity is zero — both limits follow from the formula.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: The mark is in naming θ correctly — the angle between the two transmission axes, not the angle between the light and the polaroid.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Statement of the law
lines: When plane polarised light falls on an
analyser, the intensity of the transmitted
light varies as the square of the cosine of
the angle between the transmission axes of
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words square of the cosine and transmission axes must both appear.
steps.why: The analyser passes only the component of the electric field along its axis, E₀ cos θ. Intensity goes as the square of the field, which is where the cosine squared comes from — the law is the component picture written as intensity.
common_mistakes: Writing cosine instead of the square of the cosine. The field goes as cos θ; the intensity goes as cos²θ.
Applying the law to unpolarised light. Malus law is for plane polarised light falling on an analyser; unpolarised light simply halves.

recall.must_convey: That the transmitted intensity varies as the square of the cosine of the angle between the transmission axes of the polariser and the analyser.
accept: intensity varies as cos squared theta
plane polarised light on an analyser
reject: I equals I nought cos squared theta

steps.memory_tip: Field goes as cos θ, intensity is field squared — so intensity goes as cos²θ.

steps.label: Formula with symbols
lines: where I₀ = intensity of the plane polarised
light falling on the analyser, I = intensity
of the transmitted light, and θ = the angle
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The formula alone is not enough — name I₀, I and θ.
steps.why: A formula earns its mark only when every symbol is identified. θ in particular has to be tied to the two transmission axes, because that is the definition the two limiting cases (θ = 0°, θ = 90°) are read from.
common_mistakes: Leaving the symbols unnamed, so I₀ and I could mean anything.
Swapping I and I₀. I₀ is what falls on the analyser; I is what comes through.

recall.must_convey: The formula I equals I nought cos squared theta, with I₀ the incident polarised intensity, I the transmitted intensity, and θ the angle between the axes.
accept: I equals I nought cos squared theta
I nought is the incident intensity
reject: intensity varies as the square of the cosine

steps.memory_tip: Check the formula at the two ends: θ = 0° gives all the light, θ = 90° gives none.
